query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In pre-exposure Q235 steel, the degree of corrosion degradation versus protection retention is controlled by the uniformity and integrity of the initially formed passive iron oxide film. A more homogeneous oxide layer—resulting from fewer microstructural heterogeneities such as non-metallic inclusions or high grain-boundary density—will better inhibit aggressive salt attack at high temperatures, while localized defects in the oxide film lead to accelerated corrosion via micro-galvanic effects.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as-received (pre-exposure) state with typical inclusions and grain boundary distributions.
generation.intervention: Compare samples with different surface treatments (e.g., mechanical polishing, annealing to reduce heterogeneities) to modify the uniformity of the oxide film, then subject all samples to controlled high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposures as well as room temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: The high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposure environment is expected to amplify oxide film formation dynamics and any underlying microstructural effects, whereas at room temperature, the corrosion mechanisms are less reliant on oxide film integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructural uniformity and continuity (i.e., density, adhesion, and defect distribution) of the passive iron oxide layer that forms spontaneously on Q235 steel.
generation.mechanism: Upon exposure to aggressive salt environments at elevated temperatures, the steel forms an oxide layer that can act as a protective barrier. However, pre-existing heterogeneities—such as inclusions or areas of high grain-boundary density—disrupt this film, creating weak spots that serve as sites for localized corrosion (via micro-galvanic cells). In relatively homogeneous regions, the oxide film remains coherent and retards further corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with enhanced surface uniformity (via polishing or annealing) will display a more continuous and adherent oxide layer, resulting in lower mass loss and better retention of mechanical properties (e.g., hardness) under high-temperature salt exposure compared to untreated samples. At room temperature, differences are expected to be less pronounced.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel exposed to identical environmental conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic effect is anticipated to be significant primarily under high-temperature salt exposure (700–900 °C) where oxide kinetics and film integrity are critical; at room temperature, different corrosion mechanisms may predominate.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the quantitative thresholds of microstructural heterogeneity that lead to oxide film breakdown and whether additional minor alloying elements in Q235 steel contribute significantly to film stability under cyclic thermal stresses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of Q235 steel samples: one set with a fine, uniform surface finish (polished or optimally annealed) and one with the as-received microstructure. Expose both sets to controlled salt environments at high temperatures (700–900 °C) and room temperature. Characterize the oxide film using surface microscopy and phase analysis techniques (e.g., SEM, XRD), measure mass loss, and assess mechanical properties (e.g., microhardness) before and after exposure.
measurements: Oxide film continuity and phase composition (XRD, SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the surface-treated samples do not show significantly improved oxide film uniformity and correspondingly reduced corrosion (i.e., similar mass changes and mechanical degradation as untreated specimens) under high-temperature salt exposure, or if differences between high-temperature and room temperature effects are not pronounced, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.
